I saw the buyer's draft. Before I read twelve pages, what are they asking us to do?
Mainly three things. We undertake to deliver a monitoring report within sixty days of each verification, and we commit to keeping the registry up to date.
Sixty days is fine. What else?
We have to refrain from selling the same credits to anybody else until the transfer is complete.
That worries me. What if a better buyer appears next month?
Then we would be in breach. I recommend accepting it, because after paying they are entitled to some certainty.
Can we postpone signing until the spring? The market may go up.
I would avoid postponing it. They are already seeking other projects, and they have agreed to link the payment to the issuance.
And if they object to our price review clause?
Then I suggest waiving the review for the first year only. We keep it for the years after that.

Hi Amanda, it is Ingrid, from the buyer's legal team. I promised to send the draft clause by Friday, and it is in your inbox now. Let me explain three points before you read it. First, my client has agreed to link the payment to the date the credits are issued, so we have stopped insisting on a calendar date. Second, we would like you to undertake to deliver a monitoring report within sixty days of each verification. We are not trying to control your project. We simply want to avoid paying for credits that nobody has checked. Third, and this is the sensitive one, the clause asks you to refrain from selling the same credits to anybody else until the transfer is complete. I expect your commercial team to object to that, and I am happy to discuss it. I suggest having a call on Tuesday. If Tuesday does not work, please let me know which day you prefer.

Most verbs in English take one pattern and keep it. You avoid doing something, and you agree to do something. But a few verbs change their meaning with the pattern, and in a legal document that change is a different fact. Take stop. We stopped negotiating means the negotiation ended. We stopped to negotiate means we interrupted something else in order to negotiate. Remember works the same way. I remember sending the notice is a memory about the past. I remembered to send the notice says something more useful: there was a duty, and I did not forget it. And then there is try. We tried to contact the verifier means we made an effort, and perhaps we failed. We tried contacting the verifier means it was one option among several. So my advice is simple. When stop, remember or try appears in a statement you are going to sign, read the sentence twice, and ask yourself which fact it states.

Start by saying which clause it is, and what it is about. Then say what we undertake to do. Then say what we must refrain from doing. Then say what the other side is entitled to do if we fail. And finally, give your recommendation.
